passage:
Monday. On her first day at the new school, Rukmini had four friends by lunch and a game of river-bank going by the last bell. During silent reading she tapped her pencil, swung her legs and whispered to the girl beside her, Irawati, until the teacher looked up.
Wednesday. At break Rukmini dragged Irawati into a noisy game of tag. Irawati kept glancing at the library door and said, "Maybe later," twice. Rukmini didn't hear it.
Friday. Irawati sat alone under the neem tree with a book. Rukmini ran up, then stopped, remembering Wednesday. "Do you want me to go, or sit?" "Sit, but quietly?" Rukmini sat, her knee jiggling, and lasted six whole minutes.

qa.q: How many friends did Rukmini have by lunch on Monday?
qa.a: Rukmini had four friends by lunch.

qa.q: What does Irawati glancing at the library door suggest she wanted?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable in the noisy game and wanted quiet time with books instead.

qa.q: What changed on Friday when Rukmini found Irawati alone?
qa.a: Rukmini stopped and asked whether to go or sit, choosing to respect her friend's need for space this time.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt sitting quietly beside Irawati on Friday?
qa.a: Keeping still was clearly hard for Rukmini, as the jiggling knee shows, but Rukmini may have felt glad to be allowed to stay after remembering Wednesday.

grounding: Over a week, a chatty girl who makes friends fast and fidgets in silent work learns to notice a quieter friend's need for space.

passage: You remind me of myself, Lavanya. At nine I was the loudest boy in our Mysuru school. I could make a friend at the bus stop before the bus came. In every cricket game in our lane I was captain, umpire and commentator. But in silent writing hour I felt like ants were under my skin; I'd hum, and the teacher would send me to stand outside. My best friend Raghu was the opposite. One day he told me, very softly, that he didn't want to play at recess. I laughed and pulled him along anyway. He didn't speak to me for a week. That was when I learned to hear the quiet ones, kanna. Your Naveen Thatha still talks too much, but he listens now too.

qa.q: What three roles did Naveen play in the lane cricket games?
qa.a: Captain, umpire and commentator.

qa.q: What did young Naveen feel during silent writing hour?
qa.a: He felt restless, like ants were under his skin, so he hummed.

qa.q: What turning point taught Naveen to listen to quieter friends?
qa.a: After he pulled Raghu into recess despite his soft no, Raghu stayed silent for a week, and Naveen learned to hear the quiet ones.

qa.q: How might Raghu have felt when his soft request was laughed off?
qa.a: He likely felt ignored and hurt, which is why he kept away for a week.

grounding: A grandfather recalls being a talkative boy who led games and hated silent work, and who once missed a quiet friend's cue.

passage:
Monday. By lunch on her first day at the new school, Vandana knew eleven names and was captain of the kho-kho game.
Wednesday. Silent reading. Vandana's pencil tapped, her feet swung, and she whispered jokes to the girl beside her until Mrs. Fernandes moved her desk to the front.
Saturday. Vandana's birthday: fifteen friends, music, a treasure hunt she had planned herself. Twenty minutes in, Imran's mother came to fetch him. Vandana's smile slipped. 'He didn't like it?' Later her father said, 'Did you see him by the speaker with his hands over his ears? He told you twice it was loud.' She hadn't heard. On Sunday she phoned Imran. 'Want to come over? Just us. Carrom. No music.' 'Okay,' he said, and she could hear him smiling.

qa.q: How many names did Vandana know by lunch on her first day?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when Imran left the party early?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused, her smile slipping as she wondered whether he didn't like it.

qa.q: What did Vandana's Sunday phone call get right?
qa.a: It offered Imran the kind of time he enjoys, just the two of them and no music, once she realised she had missed his cues.

qa.q: What was the party like for Imran?
qa.a: It was too loud for him; he stood by the speaker covering his ears and had said so twice, so he left early.

grounding: Shows a child who makes friends quickly, leads games and fidgets in silent work, but misses a quieter friend's cues until a parent points them out.

passage: Darshan, you talk just like I did. At your age in Ludhiana, I knew every child on our street by the second day. I picked the cricket teams and chattered through the quiet reading hour until Master ji said, 'Amandeep, one more word and you sit beside me.' But my best friend Jaspal was different. One summer he stopped coming to matches, and I kept shouting at his window, 'Come! We need you!' I thought he was sulking. Then one evening I saw him on his roof, holding his kite, not flying it. I climbed up and, for once, said nothing. Then he told me his mother was in hospital. I sat with him every evening after that. Your Nanu learned to be quiet on that roof.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep find Jaspal one evening?
qa.a: On his roof, holding his kite, not flying it.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel about Jaspal staying away from the matches at first?
qa.a: Amandeep felt impatient and a bit annoyed, thinking Jaspal was sulking, and kept shouting at his window.

qa.q: What choice on the roof changed things between the two friends?
qa.a: Amandeep climbed up and, for once, said nothing; that quiet gave Jaspal the space to share that his mother was in hospital.

qa.q: What might that summer have been like for Jaspal?
qa.a: Jaspal was worried and sad about his mother and needed quiet, so the shouts to come and play were probably hard to answer.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a talkative child who leads games and struggles in quiet hours, missing a friend's need for space until he notices it.

passage: It had rained since morning, so recess was indoors, and Ritu could hardly bear it. Forty minutes of silent seat work had left her knees jiggling under the desk. The moment the bell rang she jumped up. 'Dumb charades! Girls versus boys!' In two minutes she had teams, a scorer and a chalk list of films. Only Pallavi stayed at her desk, a library book open, not turning pages. 'Pallavi, you're on my team!' Ritu tugged her arm. 'I said I don't want to.' 'Come on, it's fun!' 'Ritu, stop.' Pallavi's voice cracked. Ritu let go. Now she saw it: the red eyes, the unturned page. Pallavi had said no twice already that morning. Ritu picked someone else for her team and sat down beside Pallavi, saying nothing.

qa.q: What game did Ritu organise?
qa.a: Dumb charades, girls versus boys.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling during the forty minutes of silent seat work?
qa.a: Ritu felt restless and bored, knees jiggling, longing for company and noise.

qa.q: What could Ritu have noticed earlier?
qa.a: That Pallavi had already said no twice and was staring at an unturned page; a quiet 'Are you okay?' before tugging her arm would have helped.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when Ritu tugged her arm?
qa.a: Pallavi felt upset and overwhelmed, her voice cracking, on a morning that was already hard.

grounding: Shows a child who gains energy from company and leads games but, restless after silent work, misses a friend's quiet cues until they become obvious.

passage: In their Delhi colony, Tenzin, ten, had organised a cricket team, a kite club and a treasure hunt, all in one summer. Everyone came to his door. But in class silent reading felt like torture; he tapped his pencil, whispered jokes and got shushed twice. At break he rushed up to Swati, who was sitting alone with a book. "Come on, we need a fielder!" She shook her head. He kept talking, about the match, the new ball, a funny video. Swati turned a page, her lips tight. Tenzin finally noticed. "You want to read, right?" She nodded. "Sorry. I'll save you a turn after lunch." Swati smiled for the first time that day.

qa.q: How many activities did Tenzin organise that summer?
qa.a: Three: a cricket team, a kite club and a treasure hunt.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel during silent reading?
qa.a: He felt restless and bored, tapping his pencil and whispering jokes.

qa.q: What did Tenzin learn to do with Swati?
qa.a: He noticed her quiet cue, her tight lips, asked what she wanted and gave her space, offering a turn later.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt while Tenzin kept talking?
qa.a: Swati probably felt crowded and a bit irritated, wanting quiet time with her book.

grounding: Shows a talkative child who leads games and is restless during silent work, energised by company but at first missing a friend's quiet cue for space.
